correctness.rationale: On the dense torus, degree-\(m\) monomial ratios generate the subgroup spanned by \(S_m-S_m\) in the primitive kernel lattice \(L\). The vectors \(u=(n^2+1,-(n^2-1),0)\) and \(v=(-n,-n,1)\) have cross product equal to the negative primitive weight vector, so they form a lattice basis. For every factorization, \(m=n^2T-D\) with \(D=x-y\) and \(T=x+y+2nz\); distinct \(D\)-levels differ by \(2n^2\), feasibility costs \(f(D)=n^2|D|-D\), and a repeated level costs an additional \(2n^3\). Three levels cost at least \(2(n^4-1)>M\); two adjacent levels with one repeated have minimum \(M=(n+1)(n^3-1)\), while the opposite repetition costs more. Thus all fibers below \(M\) are collinear. At \(M\), the three displayed exponent vectors have differences \(u,v\), proving birationality. The argument handles all even \(n\ge2\), including the boundary case \(n=2\).

value.rationale: The initiating paper explicitly identifies the actual threshold of this family as a question needed to understand the one-power gap between its necessary and sufficient birationality exponents. The exact value \(n^4+n^3-n-1\) is a natural invariant of the whole infinite sharpness family, not an arbitrary finite slice. It shows that the family's true growth exponent is \(4\), quantitatively locating it between the published \(7/2\) obstruction and \(9/2\) sufficient order and providing a concrete benchmark for improving the general conversion theorem.
